                  COMMENTS OF INVENERGY RENEWABLES LLC AND
                          INVENERGY THERMAL LLC

        Invenergy Renewables LLC and Invenergy Thermal LLC (collectively, “Invenergy”)

respectfully submit these comments in response to PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s (“PJM”) Initial

Brief in the Order to Show Cause Proceeding,1 as well as PJM’s Compliance Filing submitted in

Docket No. ER26-1479-000.2 Invenergy seeks clarification regarding the study processes for

generator interconnection and transmission service, as well as the definition of Eligible Customer.

        The Show Cause proceeding is a needed first step to address the growing demand from

manufacturing, data centers, and artificial intelligence. Invenergy applauds PJM for its

considerable work to date and raises the following issues in the interest of crafting durable and

workable rules for co-located generation and load.

        Specifically, while the purpose of PJM’s multiple filings is to facilitate co-located projects,

 PJM’s Initial Brief and compliance filings would continue to treat generator interconnection

studies and transmission service studies for co-located projects as distinct processes operating on

different timelines, rather than as a synchronized process that must be coordinated to finance and

timely construct co-located projects. As Invenergy explained in its initial comments in Docket

EL25-49, coordinating generator interconnection and transmission service studies can reduce

systemwide costs by matching generation with load, resulting in a common set of network

upgrades to accommodate both requests, and reduce the likelihood that uncoordinated study

processes result in potentially unneeded network upgrades. Synchronizing the generator

interconnection and transmission study processes would therefore provide practical benefits to

developers, who could more easily finance and bring projects online more quickly, and save

ratepayers money.

I.         COMMENTS

           A.       PJM Should Adopt a Coordinated Study Process for Co-Located Loads and
                    Generation.

           In response to the Commission’s directive to provide clear and consistent procedures for

generation serving co-located load,3 PJM submitted tariff revisions to: (1) clarify the necessary

study process for existing generation seeking to serve co-located load,4 (2) address the types of

interconnection services generators may request, including provisional5 and surplus

interconnection service,6 (3) clarify that generators may request interconnection service below

                                                             2
 their full maximum output,7 and (4) permit generators to use existing study processes to accelerate

new service requests that do not have to pay for network upgrades.8 PJM in its Initial Brief has

separately proposed the non-rate terms of service for the new firm contract, non-firm contract, and

interim NITS transmission services, including the study processes for each.9

           With limited exceptions,10 PJM’s filings perpetuate a bifurcated study process for generator

interconnection and transmission service requests. There is no requirement that the studies be done

in concert, on similar time frames, or using similar study assumptions. As a result, the distinct

studies may identify duplicative or unnecessary network upgrades, and co-located generators and

their associated load will each have to execute generator interconnection agreements or

transmission service agreements without knowing the outcome of the other study process. A co-

located generator could, for instance, be required to execute a generator interconnection agreement

without knowing whether its associated load can get transmission service at all, much less the

expected costs of any upgrades required to serve that load. Likewise, a co-located load may be

required to contract for transmission service without knowing whether the associated generation

will materialize. Given that PJM’s proposed transmission products in part anticipate co-located

loads netting their co-located generation from their transmission service requests, the failure to

coordinate these study processes may result in a cascade of restudies should load execute

transmission service agreements only to discover that the associated co-located generator cannot

 timely interconnect, or those loads will have to draw power exclusively from the grid, thereby

stressing the system in exactly the manner this proceeding is intended to prevent.

         Moreover, as a practical matter, few generation and load developers will be willing to

execute generator interconnection or transmission service agreements—and thereby commit tens,

if not hundreds of millions of dollars, to develop a project—without knowing whether it has a

reasonable prospect of moving forward; and the banks financing such projects will also be loathe

to commit capital without reviewing both generator interconnection and transmission service study

results articulating the expected cost of the project. The co-location study processes should be

designed to limit uncertainty,11 not exacerbate it. Without reforms to coordinate these study

processes, the benefits of co-location will never materialize at scale.

          Beyond these practical realities, coordinating interconnection and transmission service

studies will enhance reliability and make more efficient use of the transmission system. If

transmission service and generation interconnection are studied under two separate processes, they

could use a different set of study assumptions, models, and timelines, and therefore may each

identify network upgrades that would not be necessary were these processes coordinated.

Synchronizing the two study processes therefore comports with FERC’s goals of promoting

 efficiency and speed,12 and the Show Cause proceeding’s directive to enhance the clarity of the

co-location processes.13

           Although the Commission did not require PJM to combine transmission service and

interconnection studies into a single queue, coordination between the two processes is necessary

to effectuate the co-location arrangements contemplated by the Show Cause Order and

Replacement Rate Order. Invenergy therefore requests that the Commission and PJM clarify as

part of this proceeding how such transmission and generator interconnection study processes,

including the study processes for interconnecting new generation and modifying existing

generation, can work in tandem to provide the certainty to generators and load that is necessary to

ensure these processes work as the Commission intended.

           B.      Eligible Customer Definition As Applied Should Be Clarified.

       Consistent with the pro forma Open Access Transmission Tariff, PJM’s Tariff defines

Eligible Customer:

           (i)     Any electric utility (including any Transmission Owner and any power
                   marketer), Federal power marketing agency, or any person generating
                   electric energy for sale for resale is an Eligible Customer under the
                   Tariff. Electric energy sold or produced by such entity may be electric
                   energy produced in the United States, Canada or Mexico. However, with
                   respect to transmission service that the Commission is prohibited from
                   ordering by Section 212(h) of the Federal Power Act, such entity is
                   eligible only if the service is provided pursuant to a state requirement that
                   the Transmission Provider or Transmission Owner offer the unbundled
                   transmission service, or pursuant to a voluntary offer of such service by a
                   Transmission Owner.
           (ii)    Any retail customer taking unbundled transmission service pursuant to a
                   state requirement that the Transmission Provider or a Transmission
                   Owner offer the transmission service, or pursuant to a voluntary offer of
                   such service by a Transmission Owner, is an Eligible Customer under the
                   Tariff. As used in Tariff, Part VI, Eligible Customer shall mean only

                       those Eligible Customers that have submitted a Completed Application.14

            Invenergy seeks confirmation on how the Commission and PJM view this definition when

applied to the co-located generator and co-located load. In Order No. 888, the Commission noted

that Eligible Customers could include municipal utilities, cooperatives, investor-owned utilities,

independent power producers, and qualifying facilities, among others.15

            While the Commission cannot mandate wheeling directly to end-use customers under

Section 212(h) of the FPA, the Commission has determined that its jurisdiction extends to all

unbundled transmission in interstate commerce by public utilities.16 Thus, as provided in the

definition of Eligible Customer, where a state retail choice program results in unbundled retail

access, customers may take transmission service as an Eligible Customer.17 It is therefore

Invenergy’s understanding that a co-located load could qualify as an Eligible Customer in a retail

choice jurisdiction. In addition, Invenergy seeks clarity on the following questions:

            (1) In the context of co-location arrangements, would a co-located generator
                qualify as an Eligible Customer on behalf of the co-located load?
            (2) Does a co-located generator’s status as an Eligible Customer depend on whether
                the co-location arrangement is in a jurisdiction that has mandated retail choice?

II.         CONCLUSION
            Invenergy respectfully requests that PJM and the Commission consider these comments

and make such adjustments as necessary to ensure just and reasonable rates, terms, and conditions

for co-located arrangements.
